headline: ASX closed down 0.5% on a soft Tuesday session — PLS took the hardest hit in your portfolio, falling 3.1% as lithium sentiment stays subdued, while the US-Iran conflict continues to dominate global headlines.

movers.name: Pilbara Minerals
movers.note: PLS dropped 3.1% today — the worst mover in your portfolio. No single news catalyst, but lithium prices remain under pressure as the market works through oversupply. Analysts note the sector is 'rebalancing,' which is a polite way of saying prices haven't recovered yet. The long-term demand story — driven by EVs, semiconductors and robotics — remains intact, but patience is required.

movers.name: Global X Artificial Intelligence ETF
movers.note: GXAI slipped 1.9% today, tracking broader weakness in tech and AI stocks on the ASX. The fund holds global AI companies, so it tends to mirror US tech sentiment — which has been cautious this week. Nothing structurally wrong; AI investment spending is still accelerating globally.

movers.name: Vanguard FTSE Emerging Markets ETF
movers.note: VGE fell 0.8% today. Emerging markets copped some selling pressure — partly driven by geopolitical uncertainty around the US-Iran conflict, which tends to make investors nervous about riskier assets. The AUD nudged up slightly, which can also drag on unhedged foreign holdings.

movers.name: Vanguard US Total Market Shares ETF
movers.note: VTS dipped 0.8% today on the ASX, reflecting last night's US market close. The US total market ETF tracks the whole US sharemarket, so broad cautiousness in global equities filtered through. Still sitting 3.96% above your cost base overall — solid position.

movers.name: Vanguard Diversified High Growth ETF
movers.note: VDHG eased 0.5% today — a very minor move for a diversified fund. This one holds a mix of Aussie and global shares, so it absorbs daily volatility well. Still marginally in the green overall (+0.77% on your total investment).

movers.name: Alphabet Inc. (Google)
movers.note: No price data available for tonight — US markets haven't opened yet. Last close was USD $343.54. No specific news on Google today; watch for any AI competition updates given Alibaba's new model release.

movers.name: Microsoft
movers.note: MSFT last closed at USD $495.40. Multiple outlets are flagging Microsoft as a Q2 earnings season standout performer alongside Palantir, which is a good signal. Motley Fool published a 'buy the dip' style analysis today. US markets open tonight — worth watching.

movers.name: Take-Two Interactive
movers.note: TTWO last closed at USD $246.95 and is holding above that level according to today's coverage. GTA 6 hype is still doing the heavy lifting — analysts note the game is driving Take-Two's fiscal 2027 targets higher. Continued positive momentum ahead of the release.

watch_today.title: PLS.AX: Lithium pain continues — hold tight
watch_today.detail: Pilbara dropped 3.1% today and is now 26.9% below your purchase price — the biggest drag in the portfolio. But the long-term thesis (EV growth, battery storage, semiconductor demand) hasn't changed. Analysts are calling this a 'rebalancing' phase, not a collapse. Selling now would lock in the loss at the worst possible time. Sit tight.

watch_today.title: GXAI.AX: AI ETF softer — still a long-term hold
watch_today.detail: GXAI slipped another 1.9% today and is down 13.4% from your cost base. The fund tracks global AI companies, and while short-term sentiment has been patchy, AI capital spending by the big tech players is still accelerating. No structural reason to sell. If anything, this is the kind of dip a long-term investor watches with interest.

watch_today.title: MSFT: Q2 earnings season standout — looking strong
watch_today.detail: Multiple financial outlets today named Microsoft as one of the top Q2 earnings season performers alongside Palantir. US markets open tonight (~11:30 PM AEST) — any further positive analyst commentary could push MSFT higher in tonight's session. Your cost base is sitting around USD $443 (based on invested amount). At $495, you're well in the money. Hold and enjoy the ride.

watch_today.title: TTWO: GTA 6 narrative still driving the stock
watch_today.detail: Take-Two closed at USD $246.95 last night and analysts note it's holding above $246 with fiscal 2027 targets being lifted on the back of GTA 6 expectations. Red Bull also published a vehicle showcase article today keeping the hype cycle alive. Long-term hold — the GTA 6 launch remains the biggest catalyst in gaming.

watch_today.title: US-Iran conflict: oil at $84.95 — watch energy exposure
watch_today.detail: The US-Iran war is escalating, with Iran threatening a new offensive and the US ruling out extending a ceasefire deal. Oil (WTI) is up 0.5% to $84.95 today. Sustained conflict could push oil higher, which flows through to inflation and interest rate expectations globally. Watch this — it's the biggest macro wildcard right now.

watch_today.title: RBA rate outlook: November hike back on the table
watch_today.detail: Bendigo Bank today tipped the RBA could hike interest rates in November, even after the recent pause boosted consumer confidence. The RBA itself sounded the alarm on state government debt. Rate hikes are a headwind for growth stocks and property — worth monitoring ahead of the next RBA meeting.

world.summary: The US-Iran conflict is the dominant global story today, with Iran threatening escalation and the US refusing to extend any ceasefire. Meanwhile, Trump's push to control federal elections is drawing scrutiny, and geopolitical tensions continue to rattle markets.

stories.title: Iran threatens new offensive as US rules out ceasefire extension
stories.why_it_matters: Iran has threatened to launch a new military offensive while the US has firmly ruled out extending any ceasefire agreement. This is a significant escalation — it means active conflict between the US and Iran could intensify in the coming days. For everyday people, this matters because sustained conflict in the Middle East pushes oil prices higher (already up to $84.95 today), which flows through to petrol prices and global inflation. It also makes financial markets nervous, which is why you saw broad selling today.

stories.title: Iran's secret plan to escalate the war
stories.why_it_matters: The Wall Street Journal reports Iran has a secret plan to escalate beyond current military operations — the details aren't fully public, but it signals Iran isn't looking to de-escalate. The US CENTCOM chief (America's top Middle East military commander) visited troops aboard the USS Abraham Lincoln amid morale concerns, suggesting the conflict is taking a real toll on US forces. This is a live, developing war — not just sabre-rattling.

stories.title: Iran's rulers wary of economic collapse and unrest as US pressure builds
stories.why_it_matters: Despite the tough talk, Reuters reports Iran's leadership is deeply worried about the war's economic damage — sanctions and conflict have battered the Iranian economy, and there are real fears of domestic unrest if conditions worsen. This is actually important context: it suggests Iran may be in a weaker position than its rhetoric implies, and there could eventually be pressure to negotiate. But in the short term, desperation can make states more dangerous, not less.

stories.title: Trump's push to seize control of federal elections faces a ticking clock
stories.why_it_matters: The Trump administration is reportedly pushing hard to gain greater federal control over how US elections are run — a move critics say could undermine independent state-level election oversight. The article notes time pressure, suggesting legal or legislative deadlines are looming. This matters because US political stability has direct consequences for global markets — uncertainty around the 2026 and 2028 electoral cycle is already a background risk factor investors are watching.

indicators.name: AUD/USD

politics.summary: The RBA and interest rates are dominating domestic headlines today — with consumer confidence improving after the recent rate pause, but some banks now tipping a November hike. Labor also killed off the so-called 'widow tax' after months of backlash, and gambling ad reforms are close to a bipartisan deal.

stories.title: RBA rate pause boosts consumer confidence — but November hike looms
stories.why_it_matters: Australian consumer confidence has improved following the RBA's decision to hold interest rates — people are feeling a little better about spending and their finances. But the good news may be short-lived: Bendigo Bank today tipped the RBA could still hike rates in November, and the Canberra Times reports the RBA itself is 'not ruling out' further increases. For mortgage holders, this is the key story to watch — a November hike would push repayments up again just as people were starting to breathe easier.

stories.title: RBA sounds alarm on state government debt binge
stories.why_it_matters: The Reserve Bank has warned that Australian state governments are borrowing too heavily — a 'debt binge' that could add to inflationary pressures and complicate the RBA's job of bringing inflation down. When states borrow and spend big, it pumps money into the economy, which can work against the RBA's interest rate policy. It's a tension between federal monetary policy (RBA) and state-level fiscal spending — and it matters for how long rates stay elevated.

stories.title: Labor kills off 'widow tax' after months of backlash
stories.why_it_matters: The Labor government has scrapped a policy that critics dubbed the 'widow tax' — a rule that reduced pension payments for surviving spouses, particularly older women who lost a partner. After months of public backlash, Labor has backed down. It's a win for affected retirees and a sign that the government is sensitive to cost-of-living pressures on vulnerable Australians ahead of any future election cycle.

stories.title: Labor and Coalition close to bipartisan deal on gambling ad reforms
stories.why_it_matters: Labor and the Coalition are reportedly close to striking a bipartisan deal on gambling advertising reforms, which would allow Australians to opt out of all gambling ads. The AFR reports the opt-out system is coming soon — a significant change for anyone who watches sport and gets bombarded with betting ads. For media companies and betting firms, this is a headwind; for ordinary sports fans, it's potentially welcome relief.

ai.summary: Today's AI news is dominated by the regulatory debate — how to govern AI without strangling it — plus Alibaba firing back at Meta with a new locally-runnable model, and a fresh benchmark comparison of the latest Claude, GPT, and Gemini models.

stories.title: Alibaba launches new AI model that runs on a laptop — taking aim at Meta
stories.why_it_matters: Alibaba has released a new AI model designed to run directly on a laptop — no cloud server required. This is a direct challenge to Meta's locally-runnable Llama models. What it means in practice: you could run a powerful AI assistant on your own computer without sending data to anyone else, which is a big deal for privacy and for users in areas with poor internet. Chinese tech companies are increasingly competitive with US AI labs — not just copying, but innovating.

stories.title: Claude Sonnet 5 vs GPT-5.6 vs Gemini 3.7 Flash: the latest AI model shootout
stories.why_it_matters: Tech-insider.org published a fresh head-to-head comparison of the three leading AI assistants: Anthropic's Claude Sonnet 5, OpenAI's GPT-5.6, and Google's Gemini 3.7 Flash. A separate comparison of Claude Fable 5 vs GPT-5.6 reportedly showed a '13x gap' in performance on certain tasks. This matters for your GOOG holding — Google's Gemini needs to stay competitive with OpenAI and Anthropic, and these benchmark comparisons are how the market judges who's winning the AI race.

stories.title: Growing calls to regulate AI in finance to protect consumers
stories.why_it_matters: New research is urging regulators to impose rules on how AI is used in financial services — things like robo-advisers, credit decisions, and fraud detection. The concern is that AI systems can make biased or opaque decisions that hurt consumers, and right now there's little oversight. For investors in AI-exposed stocks and ETFs like GXAI, heavier regulation could slow deployment in the finance sector — but it could also create more trust and wider adoption long-term.

stories.title: AI regulation is in flux — what should businesses do now?
stories.why_it_matters: With AI rules changing rapidly across different countries and industries, businesses are being urged to get ahead of compliance requirements now rather than scrambling later. The key insight: AI regulation is becoming a genuine business risk, not just a theoretical concern. For AI-focused ETFs and tech stocks in your portfolio, regulatory clarity (when it comes) could actually be a positive — it removes uncertainty and lets companies plan with confidence.

sport.summary: NRL Round 25 is on the horizon with some big team news — Manly making a call on Tom Trbojevic, the Tigers suffering a brutal blow, and the Storm poaching a key forward. In AFL, Brisbane Lions need a win to hold their top-four spot, and the Sydney Swans are dealing with a serious off-field police investigation.

stories.title: Manly's big Turbo call and brutal Tigers blow ahead of Round 25
stories.why_it_matters: Fox Sports reports Manly coach Anthony Seibold is facing a big decision on whether to play Tom Trbojevic (Turbo) in Round 25, while the Wests Tigers are copping a brutal injury blow ahead of their Sunday clash with the Roosters at Allianz Stadium. Specific injury details weren't available, but Fox Sports flagged coach Madge is making major selection moves. With the Tigers already out of finals contention, any further disruption is a blow to their momentum for next season.

stories.title: Melbourne Storm poach key forward from Sydney rival ahead of 2027
stories.why_it_matters: The Melbourne Storm have locked in a surprise forward signing from a Sydney club for 2027, and also secured another player in what's shaping up as a strong off-season recruitment drive. The Storm host the Panthers on Thursday night at AAMI Park in the Round 25 opener — the squad depth news is timely with finals positioning on the line.

stories.title: Sydney Swans players under police investigation over sexual assault claim
stories.why_it_matters: Police are investigating multiple Sydney Swans AFL players over a sexual assault allegation — a serious off-field matter that has reached international coverage via the BBC. The club hasn't confirmed how many players are involved or whether anyone will be stood down. With finals approaching, this is a significant cloud over the Swans' season and the AFL's reputation more broadly.

stories.title: Brisbane Lions need a win to hold top-four spot — Fagan unfazed by Collingwood selection puzzle
stories.why_it_matters: Brisbane Lions coach Chris Fagan says he's relaxed about Collingwood's selection decisions ahead of their clash, with Brisbane needing the win to protect their top-four finals position. The Lions are in a tight battle for the double chance — a top-four spot means a home final and two shots at making the Grand Final. Fagan's calm public demeanour suggests the Lions camp is confident despite the stakes.

stories.title: Sabalenka reveals Djokovic slid into her DMs during Cincinnati Open
stories.why_it_matters: World No. 1 Aryna Sabalenka revealed at the Cincinnati Open that Novak Djokovic sent her a direct message — and she joked 'he was begging.' The light-hearted story comes as Sabalenka is in fine form at Cincinnati. The tournament is a key US Open warmup event, and Sabalenka is among the favourites for the US Open title later this month.
